title: Power For Rather than Power Over
author: Kathleen Schafer
summary: Kathleen Schafer's letter to soulful leaders begins with Robert Fulghum's decades-old observation: societies treat care as expensive while rarely questioning spending on domination and destruction. Schafer draws on Riane Eisler's The Chalice and the Blade to name the civilizational dynamic: societies organized around 'power over' rather than 'power for' prioritize the ability to take life over the ability to give it. The essay applies this analysis to leadership: Step Five of the Leadership Connection Model is Building Team, which requires leaders to move from individual excellence to collective capacity. Schafer argues that the current moment demands leaders who build coalitions and care structures, not just command hierarchies. The piece weaves civic, relational, and leadership concerns into a coherent argument for a different model of power -- one oriented toward enabling others rather than controlling them.
points: * Societies organized around 'power over' -- domination, control, punishment -- devalue the care work that sustains human life; this is a values failure visible in budget priorities. * Riane Eisler's framework names the dynamic: the turn from life-giving to life-taking power is not inevitable but the result of historical choices that can be made differently. * Effective leadership in the current moment requires 'power for' -- building capacity, enabling others, creating conditions for collective flourishing rather than asserting hierarchical control. * Step Five of the Leadership Connection Model (Building Team) is the move from individual excellence to collaborative capacity; expansion is not a solo act. * The question 'With whom are we building?' is the essential leadership question for the current moment; answering it requires both self-knowledge and genuine commitment to others' development.
quotes: Dear Soulful Leaders, After reading the headlines recently, I recalled a quote I first saw early in my career: "It will be a great day when our schools get all the money they need, and the Air Force has to hold a bake sale to buy a bomber." Robert Fulghum wrote those words more than four decades ago.
We rarely question what we spend to dominate, punish, and destroy.
The cost of healing, educating, housing, feeding, and supporting human beings gets debated as though care itself is the indulgence.
Riane Eisler named it clearly in The Chalice and the Blade: the civilizational turn that happened when the ability to take life became more valued than the ability to give it.
We are watching what happens when societies organize themselves around power over rather than power for, around domination rather than care, around control rather than the capacity to uplift life.
Which is why Step Five of the Leadership Connection Model, Building Team, matters so much right now.
Once we know who we are, name what we want to contribute, align our lives with what we value, and practice the skills of leadership, the next question becomes: With whom are we building?
